\chapter{Neither This Nor That}
\label{ch:ml-neither}
\hlchaptermodality{109}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can deny a pair of things at once, and pick the right negative for what I am denying.}

From cold: both shapes of neither-nor, and the question English never makes you answer.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[caayayum kaappiyum illa]{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല} — neither of them is here}

\label{lesson:ML-C109-neither-here}



\begin{quote}
Join two things with the ending you know: \emph{tea and coffee}.

Then say the word for \emph{there isn't any}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{cāyayum kāppiyum illa} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{There is neither tea nor coffee.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Nothing in that sentence is new.} You built \textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും}} when you learned to join two things, and \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} has been yours since your first conversation. Put the one in front of the other and Malayalam has said \emph{neither}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: English buys a special word for this and Malayalam does not}]
English reaches for a pair of words it keeps only for this job — \emph{neither … nor} — and they behave unlike anything else in the sentence.

Malayalam spends nothing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും}} & the joining you already do \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} & the negative you already have \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The list is built the ordinary way, with the ending on \textbf{every} item, and then the whole list is denied at once. What English treats as a special construction, Malayalam treats as a list that happens to end in a negative.

\textbf{Both items are inside the denial}, which is the thing to hear. You are not saying \emph{there is no tea, and coffee}. The ending has tied the two together before \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} arrives, so the negative lands on the pair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tea and coffee} — \textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും}}
  \item the same pair, denied — \textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല}}
  \item which part of that sentence ties the two things together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Malayalam say \emph{neither tea nor coffee}? (\textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല}}.) How many new words did that need? (\textbf{None} — the joining ending and the negative, both already yours.) Does the negative land on one item or the pair? (\textbf{The pair.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adhyaapakanum vaidyanum alla]{\ml{അധ്യാപകനും} \ml{വൈദ്യനും} \ml{അല്ല} — neither of them is what you called it}

\label{lesson:ML-C109-neither-so}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{neither tea nor coffee}.

Then say which of your two negatives denies that a thing is \textbf{there}, and which denies that a thing is \textbf{so}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അധ്യാപകനും} \ml{വൈദ്യനും} \ml{അല്ല}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{adhyāpakanum vaidyanum alla} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}He{]} is neither a teacher nor a doctor.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same joining ending on each item. Different word at the end.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the choice you learned does not go away}]
You were told that Malayalam makes you pick a negative where English spends one word on both. \textbf{That decision survives into this construction}, and English's \emph{neither … nor} hides it completely:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല}} & neither is \textbf{there} \\
\textbf{\ml{അധ്യാപകനും} \ml{വൈദ്യനും} \ml{അല്ല}} & neither is \textbf{what you called it} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An English speaker says \emph{neither … nor} for both rows and never notices a question was asked. You have to answer it before you can finish the sentence — and the question is the same one as ever: are you denying that something is present, or denying that something is so?

\textbf{The joining half does not change.} Only the last word does, which is worth noticing: the work of coordinating stayed where it was, and all the difficulty lives in the negative.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{neither a teacher nor a doctor} — \textbf{\ml{അധ്യാപകനും} \ml{വൈദ്യനും} \ml{അല്ല}}
  \item the tea-and-coffee sentence, and say which negative it ends in
  \item which negative you would reach for to deny that two people are in the room
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part of the sentence changes between the two kinds of \emph{neither}? (\textbf{Only the last word} — the joining is identical.) Which negative denies that something is present? (\textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}}.) Which denies that something is what you called it? (\textbf{\ml{അല്ല}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[randum alla, randum illa]{(neither … nor) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R109-neither-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{neither tea nor coffee}, then \emph{neither a teacher nor a doctor}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one joining, two endings}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ചായയും} \ml{കാപ്പിയും} \ml{ഇല്ല}} & neither is there \\
\textbf{\ml{അധ്യാപകനും} \ml{വൈദ്യനും} \ml{അല്ല}} & neither is so \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The left half of those two sentences is built the same way.} Every item takes the joining ending, and the pair is denied as a pair. What differs is the last word, and picking it is the same decision you have been making since you owned two negatives.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could join things and you could deny things, and you had never been shown that doing both at once needs nothing further.} English keeps a special pair of words for this and teaches them as their own lesson. Malayalam had already given you every piece; what was missing was the sentence that puts them together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item both sentences, one after the other
  \item how many new words this chapter asked you to learn
  \item the question you answer before choosing the last word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Malayalam put on each item of the pair? (\textbf{The joining ending.}) What decides the final word? (\textbf{Whether you deny that something is there, or that something is so.}) Which English words does this replace? (\emph{\textbf{Neither … nor}} — and Malayalam spends no new word on them.)
\end{tcolorbox}
